lead: A satellite navigation receiver listens to coded radio signals from spacecraft whose orbits it already knows. It measures how long each signal took to arrive, turns each time into a range, and solves the ranges together to find its own position. The receiver's own clock is cheap, so its offset is solved as a fourth unknown. GPS — the American system whose programme name is NAVSTAR — guides airliners, ships, cars and phones, and its timing output also runs bank networks, UPI switches and power grids.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for frames and position fixing, and 5.2 for time-based ranging from a point source.

sections.h3: The NAVSTAR constellation and its orbits

blocks.text: GPS is the United States satellite navigation system; its original programme name is NAVSTAR. The baseline design places 24 satellites in 6 orbital planes, each plane inclined at 55° to the equator, at an altitude of about 20,200 km. More satellites are flown than the baseline, so a receiver on the ground usually sees 6 to 12 at a time.

Each satellite moves on a Keplerian ellipse described by six elements: semi-major axis a, eccentricity e, inclination i, right ascension of ascending node Ω, argument of perigee ω and true anomaly ν. The broadcast ephemeris lets the receiver rebuild this orbit and compute where the satellite was at the instant it transmitted.

blocks.where: T is the orbital period in seconds, a is the semi-major axis in metres and μ = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² is the Earth's gravitational constant. With a ≈ 26,560 km, T ≈ 11 h 58 min.

blocks.text: That period is half a sidereal day. After one sidereal day the Earth has turned once and the satellite has completed two orbits, so it sits over the same ground point again: the ground track repeats, and the sky geometry above a fixed site repeats too. Surveyors use this. A period of exactly 12 h solar would drift about four minutes a day and the track would not close.

sections.h3: PRN codes and the navigation message

blocks.text: All satellites share the same carrier frequencies: L1 at 1575.42 MHz, L2 at 1227.60 MHz and L5 at 1176.45 MHz. They are told apart by code. Each satellite carries its own pseudo-random noise (PRN) sequence, and a receiver separates them by correlating with the right copy — code division multiple access, CDMA.

Two codes ride on L1. The coarse/acquisition (C/A) code runs at 1.023 Mchip/s with 1023 chips, so it repeats every 1 ms. The precision P code runs at 10.23 Mchip/s and repeats weekly; it is encrypted as Y for authorised users. One C/A chip lasts 1/(1.023 × 10⁶) s ≈ 977.5 ns, which is 293 m of range, and the receiver resolves a small fraction of a chip by watching the correlation peak.

The navigation message is a 50 bit/s data stream. It carries the satellite's own ephemeris, the almanac of coarse orbits for the whole constellation, clock correction coefficients, ionospheric model coefficients and health flags. A full message takes 12.5 minutes, but one ephemeris set is enough for a first fix.

blocks.where: ρ is the pseudorange in metres, c = 299,792,458 m/s, t_receive is the arrival time read on the receiver clock and t_transmit is the transmission time read on the satellite clock. Both clocks are imperfect, so ρ is not the true geometric range.

blocks.text: For a satellite at (x_s, y_s, z_s) and a receiver at (x, y, z) the geometric range is r = √((x − x_s)² + (y − y_s)² + (z − z_s)²). The unknowns are x, y, z and the receiver clock offset δt. Each satellite gives one equation, ρ = r + c δt plus small propagation terms.

items: Track four or more satellites and decode each ephemeris.
Compute every satellite position at its transmission time.
Measure code phase and form each pseudorange.
Start from an approximate position and clock offset.
Linearise, solve for the corrections, iterate until they are small.
Output x, y, z, δt and the dilution of precision.

blocks.text: The equations are nonlinear, so the receiver linearises about its guess and builds the geometry matrix H, one row per satellite: a unit line-of-sight vector plus a 1 in the clock column. It then solves Δx = (HᵗH)⁻¹ Hᵗ Δρ and repeats. The same (HᵗH)⁻¹ gives the dilution of precision (DOP): large DOP means satellites are bunched together and every range error is stretched into a bigger position error.

GPS has three segments. The space segment is the satellites. The control segment is a master control station with monitor stations and upload antennas; it tracks the satellites, computes orbit and clock corrections, and uploads them. The user segment is every receiver, from a phone to an aircraft GNSS unit feeding the flight management system.

Other constellations work the same way with different details. GLONASS uses frequency division (FDMA, a different channel per satellite) and a 64.8° inclination that favours high latitudes. Galileo serves Europe, BeiDou serves China. NavIC is India's regional system: geostationary plus inclined geosynchronous satellites covering India and the surrounding region on L5 and S-band.

Augmentation improves accuracy and integrity. Satellite-based augmentation (SBAS) — GAGAN in India, WAAS in the United States, EGNOS in Europe — broadcasts corrections and integrity flags from a geostationary satellite over a whole region. Ground-based augmentation (GBAS) does the same from an airport for precision approach. Aircraft-based augmentation (ABAS) is receiver-side monitoring such as RAIM, which checks the measurements against each other.

figure.caption: The receiver tracks a PRN code, measures its code phase to build a pseudorange, and solves four pseudoranges for position plus receiver clock bias.

spec.title: From broadcast code to position
spec.aria: The receiver chain from a satellite broadcasting a coded signal with its own clock and orbit, through correlation and pseudorange, to a four-unknown solution giving position and receiver clock bias.

examples.question: A GPS satellite is at a slant range of 20,200 km from a receiver. (a) How long does its signal take to arrive? (b) The receiver clock is fast by 3 µs; what range error does that add to every pseudorange? (c) Why does the receiver need four satellites rather than three?
steps: Data: slant range R = 20,200 km = 2.0200 × 10⁷ m; speed of light c = 299,792,458 m/s; clock offset Δt = 3 µs = 3 × 10⁻⁶ s.
In milliseconds: 0.06738 × 1000 = 67.4 ms, so the signal left the satellite 67.4 ms before it reached the antenna.
The reading is too late by 3 µs, so every measured travel time and every pseudorange is too long by about 899 m — the same error on all four, which the fourth unknown absorbs.
(c) The unknowns are x, y, z and δt, that is four. Each satellite supplies one equation, so four satellites give four equations. Three would do only if the receiver clock were perfect.
examples.answer: The signal takes 0.0674 s (67.4 ms); the 3 µs clock error adds about 899.4 m (roughly 0.9 km) to every pseudorange; and four satellites are needed because the receiver clock offset is the fourth unknown.
examples.check:
c = 299_792_458.0
R = 20_200e3
t = R / c
print(round(t, 4))
print(round(c * 3e-6, 1))

traps: Pseudorange is not the geometric range. It carries the receiver clock offset and the propagation delays; writing ρ = r as if the clocks were perfect throws away the reason for the fourth satellite.

Three satellites give three equations but there are four unknowns, x, y, z and δt. The classic wrong answer says three spheres intersect at two points and one is rejected — true only with a perfect clock.
Do not mix the carrier with the code. L1 is 1575.42 MHz; the C/A chip rate is 1.023 Mchip/s, exactly 1/1540 of it. One C/A chip is about 293 m, one L1 cycle only 0.19 m.
24 is a baseline design figure, not the number currently flying. An answer that says GPS always has exactly 24 satellites loses marks.
DOP is geometry, not an error source. It multiplies the range error; it cannot create one, and a low DOP cannot rescue a biased pseudorange.

quiz.q: State the L1 carrier frequency and the C/A code chip rate of GPS.
quiz.a: L1 = 1575.42 MHz; C/A code = 1.023 Mchip/s, with 1023 chips repeating every 1 ms.

quiz.q: Name the three GPS segments and one element of each.
quiz.a: Space segment — the satellite constellation; control segment — master control station, monitor stations and upload antennas; user segment — receivers such as an aircraft GNSS unit.

quiz.q: Why does a satellite period of 11 h 58 min give a repeating ground track?
quiz.a: The period is half a sidereal day. In one sidereal day the Earth turns once and the satellite completes two orbits, so it returns over the same ground point and the sky geometry at a fixed site repeats.

quiz.q: Why does the receiver solve for its clock offset instead of carrying an atomic clock like the satellites?
quiz.a: An atomic standard is too costly and bulky for a receiver. Treating the offset δt as a fourth unknown removes the clock error from the answer, at the price of one extra satellite.

quiz.q: Compute the length in metres of one C/A code chip and the travel time it represents.
quiz.a: Chip duration = 1 / (1.023 × 10⁶) s = 977.5 ns. Length = 299,792,458 × 977.5 × 10⁻⁹ = 293.1 m. One chip is about 0.98 µs and 293 m.

quiz.q: RAIM needs five satellites to detect a faulty measurement and six to exclude it. Why?
quiz.a: Four measurements are fully consumed by the position and clock solution, leaving no redundancy. A fifth gives one spare for a consistency check; a sixth lets the faulty satellite be dropped and a fix still formed from the remaining four.

quiz.q: Why can one geostationary SBAS satellite such as GAGAN serve India continuously, while the GPS ranging satellites are not geostationary?
quiz.a: SBAS sends corrections and integrity for a wide region, so one fixed satellite can broadcast to the whole region all the time. Ranging satellites must move to give changing geometry and several visible satellites; a geostationary ranger would sit on the equator with poor geometry and no coverage near the poles.

beyond: Not for the exam. Multi-constellation receivers now track GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou and NavIC together, which raises the satellite count and lowers DOP. The L5 band and dual-frequency ionosphere-free combinations push stand-alone accuracy from metres to decimetres, and precise point positioning with real-time correction streams reaches centimetres. Search for multi-GNSS, PPP-RTK, NavIC augmentation and GAGAN if you want to follow this further.
